Let's talk about idempotency — one of those concepts that sounds intimidating but is surprisingly simple once it clicks.

An operation is idempotent if doing it once has the same effect as doing it many times. Think of an elevator button: pressing "5" ten times doesn't send you to the fiftieth floor.

Why does this matter? In distributed systems, networks fail. Requests time out. Clients retry. If your payment endpoint isn't idempotent, a single retry could charge a customer twice.

The common fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique ID with each request, and the server remembers which IDs it has already processed. Same key, same result, no duplicate side effects.

Small design choice, big impact on reliability.

#SoftwareEngineering #APIs #DistributedSystems

text:
A colleague asked me last week why adding an index made one of our queries slower. Fair question.

The index was on a status column with three possible values, and about 80% of rows were 'active'. When the planner used the index for status = 'active', it ended up doing a lookup per row instead of just scanning the table sequentially, which is cheaper when you're reading most of it anyway.

We dropped that index and added a partial one covering only the rare statuses. The slow query went back to a sequential scan, and the reports that filter on 'failed' got about forty times faster.

Indexes help when they narrow things down. If they don't, they're overhead.

text:
Embeddings are one of the most powerful ideas in modern AI — and they're easier to understand than you might think.

At their core, embeddings turn something messy (a sentence, an image, a product) into a list of numbers. The magic is in how those numbers are arranged: things with similar meaning end up close together in space.

So “How do I reset my password?” and “I forgot my login” land near each other, even though they share almost no words.

This unlocks a whole range of use cases:
→ Semantic search that understands intent
→ Recommendations based on meaning, not just keywords
→ Clustering support tickets to spot emerging issues

If you're building with LLMs, understanding embeddings isn't optional — it's foundational.

text:
Technical debt gets a bad reputation, but not all debt is bad debt.

Like financial debt, technical debt can be a smart strategic tool. Taking a shortcut to hit a launch window, validate an idea, or learn from real users can be exactly the right call. The problem isn’t taking on debt — it’s failing to track it and pay it down.

A few practices that have worked well for our team:

– Log shortcuts as tickets the moment you take them
– Reserve roughly 15–20% of each sprint for cleanup
– Revisit the debt backlog during quarterly planning, not just when something breaks

The goal isn’t zero debt. It’s intentional debt.

#SoftwareDevelopment #EngineeringLeadership #TechDebt

A few habits that have helped me:

📝 Write for someone joining the team six months from now
📝 Cut every sentence that doesn't earn its place

Good code solves today's problem. Good writing helps your team solve tomorrow's.
